Sojourner Truth. Born Isabella Baumfree around 1797, the African American abolitionist and women's rights activist who escaped slavery in New York and became a powerful orator.

Truth escaped to freedom in 1826 with her infant daughter. She worked as a domestic servant and preacher. In the eighteen-forties, she took the name Sojourner Truth, describing herself as a wanderer spreading the truth of God and human equality.

In 1851, she delivered what would become her most famous speech at the Women's Rights Convention in Akron, Ohio. She challenged the idea that women were too delicate for equality by pointing to her own life—her work as a slave and as a field laborer. She asked, "Ain't I a Woman?" That rhetorical question exposed the racism within the women's movement by calling attention to the erasure of Black women's experiences.

Truth traveled throughout the North speaking against slavery, for women's rights, and for Black civil rights. She often faced hostile audiences and violence. After emancipation came in 1865, she continued advocating for land redistribution and education for freed people, connecting liberation struggles across race and gender. She lived to be eighty-six, dedicating her life to the proposition that freedom must be won for all marginalized people, or truly for none.
